summary: Theo and Rae compare fragments from the Desert Marker and realize they remember incompatible emotional versions of the same event. Adrian refuses to decide which memory is true. A shared remembered phrase pulls both of them into the past.

In the forgotten past, Starbreaker presses Mero for authority to end the Desert Marker threat decisively before it spreads. Mero stalls because Redlin has asked for one final chance to contain the crisis.

Redlin enters as a full person, not an opposing symbol. He and Starbreaker reveal an old rivalry built on mutual familiarity: Starbreaker believes Redlin keeps catastrophes alive by refusing decisive endings; Redlin believes Starbreaker creates new catastrophes every time he calls one finished.

Redlin takes Mero through a civilian shelter rather than arguing from a command room. His containment position becomes human: he knows the names of people who will die if Starbreaker acts now, and he refuses to treat their deaths as proof of resolve.

Starbreaker takes Mero to the ridge and shows him what waiting has already cost elsewhere. His decisiveness is rooted in accumulated failure, not appetite for destruction. Mero sees why people follow him even when they fear him.

Mero tries to broker a pause. Starbreaker and Redlin reveal that they have had versions of this argument many times before, and both believe the other has mistaken a recurring failure for a principle.
Redlin personally holds the outer line long enough for civilians to move. The sequence defines containment as an act of protection and endurance rather than a system setting or technical field.
Starbreaker and Redlin meet alone before the final break. Their hostility briefly falls away and the reader sees the old respect underneath it. Each asks the other to stop. Neither can.

The crisis crosses the point where every available choice carries catastrophe. Mero makes no clean declaration of victory; Starbreaker acts, Redlin continues trying to contain the consequences, and the sky begins to break.

Glass dust and violet light fall over the ruined battlefield. Starbreaker believes he prevented something worse; Redlin is looking at the people who still died. Mero understands that both statements can be true, and that this is what makes the war dangerous.

Theo and Rae return to the present carrying different emotional residues from the same memory. Theo remembers Starbreaker's fear of waiting; Rae remembers the civilians Redlin was trying to move. Neither understands why the same scene belongs to both of them.

Theo and Rae press Adrian on how two people can remember private details from the same forgotten day. Adrian refuses the identity truth, but confirms that neither memory is false. The issue ends with the unsettling possibility that perspective, not accuracy, is what divides them.
